facts.fact: Betta splendens is a bubble nester: the male builds a nest of air bubbles coated with saliva, often next to something that breaks the water surface.
Male bettas may build nests with no female around, but a female swimming past often makes him build fast.
Warm water makes betta males build nests more often.
How big the nest is does not directly match how many eggs there are.
A betta female ready to spawn turns darker and shows vertical 'breeding bars'. The male courts her by flaring his gill covers and spreading his fins.
Seriously Fish says a ready betta female turns paler, with dark bars on her flanks.
Bettas spawn in an embrace under the nest, with the male wrapped around the female. Each embrace releases about 10–40 eggs.
Sources give a total of 12 to 492 eggs per betta female.
The betta male picks up sinking eggs in his mouth and puts them in the bubble nest.
UF/IFAS says bettas are bred in small containers of 3.78–18.90 liters, one male and one female, with floating plants and/or a small piece of Styrofoam for the male to build his nest under.
Give the betta female cover in the spawning tank, such as plastic tubes or empty film canisters.
After spawning, the betta female is usually taken out, because she may eat the eggs and the male may kill her if she stays.
Seriously Fish says the betta pair can usually stay together after spawning, with the male guarding the nest alone.
The betta male guards the eggs, repairs the nest and puts back any eggs or fry that fall out.
Betta eggs hatch after 24–36 hours.
Betta eggs hatch in 24 to 48 hours. The fry then stay in the nest for 3 to 4 more days until the yolk sac is used up.
Betta larvae stay in the nest for 2–3 days, until the yolk sac is absorbed, and then swim freely.
Betta fry breathe with their gills until the labyrinth organ forms at about 3–6 weeks of age.
A close-fitting lid helps betta fry: they need humid air above the water for the labyrinth organ to develop.
For the first few days, feed betta fry infusoria-sized food. After that, feed moving foods such as microworms and Artemia nauplii.
Some reports link feeding too much Artemia to health problems in young bettas.
For betta fry, Seriously Fish advises small, regular water changes rather than large, occasional ones.
Seriously Fish says adult bettas don't usually eat their young.
A betta female needs at least four weeks of rest before spawning again. Spawning sooner can give no eggs or eggs that don't develop.
A betta male needs about a week before he can fertilize eggs again.
Young bettas can usually be sexed at about two months and can be mature as early as 4–5 months.
Microworms are less than 3 mm long and keep moving, which makes them a good first food for larval fish. They are cheaper and less work than newly hatched Artemia.
UF/IFAS warns that microworms are not a complete diet for every species and should be used case by case.
Microworms are grown on a mix of oatmeal, yeast and water, 1 to 4 cm deep in a shallow container 6 to 10 cm high. The ideal temperature is 21°C to 27°C.
A 20 x 30 cm microworm culture gives about 5 to 8 mL of worms a day. Scrape the worms off the container sides and feed them without washing.
If the medium is refreshed, a microworm culture lasts up to 3 months at 20°C but only 6 weeks at 28°C. In a hot climate, expect to restart cultures more often.
Guppies bear live young. Gestation is 20 to 60 days at 25 to 27.8 °C and also depends on other conditions.
A guppy female drops 2 to 200 fry at a time, usually 30 to 60, one by one over about one to six hours.
Guppy females can store sperm and use it to fertilize eggs for up to eight months, so one mating can give several broods.
Guppy females first give birth at 10 to 20 weeks of age. Males mature in 7 weeks or less.
Guppies prefer 22.2 to 26.1 °C for breeding.
Well-fed adult guppies rarely eat their young, but fry sometimes need safe hiding places. Cannibalism rises when fish are crowded.
Discus parents secrete a skin mucus ('discus milk') that the fry feed on during their first four weeks. Both parents care for the young.
Discus fry stay attached to the cone where the eggs were laid for about the first 3 days, living on their yolk until they can swim.
In weeks 1–2, discus fry feed on the parents' mucus, sometimes for up to 10 minutes at a time.
In week 3, discus parents start swimming away for short periods. By week 4 they spend most of their time away from the brood, and the fry barely bite them.
Antibody and protein levels in discus mucus rise sharply at spawning, much like mammal milk, and fall back to normal in week 4.
Discus parents pass helpful microorganisms to their fry through their mucus. Fry raised by their parents survive much better than fry raised artificially on egg yolk or brine shrimp.
For blue discus eggs and larvae, a pH of 6.3 to 6.6 was found best for lowering stress and skeletal deformities.
Discus pairs move away from the group to breed, possibly to cut down on the young being eaten. Discus mature at about one year.
Vietnamese terms from the betta thread: 'cá cái' or 'cá mái' = female, 'tổ bọt' = bubble nest, 'cá bột' = fry, 'bơi tự do' = free-swimming.

Vietnamese terms from the discus thread: 'cá dĩa bồ câu' = pigeon blood discus, 'nhớt' = body mucus fed to fry, 'ấp nhân tạo' = artificial rearing, 'nuôi vú' = foster parenting by other discus such as brown or turquoise discus.
